ABSTRACT: In this study, atomic level interactions of a 1:1 choline chloride (ChCl)/acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) therapeutic deep eutectic solvent (THDES) has been investigated by combining the molecular dynamics (MD), density functional theory (DFT), and spectroscopic (Raman and IR) techniques. Atom-atom radial distribution functions (RDFs) based on MD simulation reveal that hydrogen bonds are formed between Cl⁻···HOch⁺ and Cl⁻···HOCOOH of the THDES, where Cl⁻ works as a bridge between ASA and Ch⁺. Cation-anion electrostatic attractions are disrupted by highly interconnected hydrogen bonds. Charge transfer calculations, using CHEPLG and NBO analysis, disclose that the charge of Cl⁻ is reduced in the cluster structures and transferred to Ch⁺ and ASA. Further analyses are conducted using experimental and computed spectroscopic data. These confirm the formation of the THDES as peaks for –COOH, –COOR, and –OH functional groups of ASA and ChCl are either get broadened or disappeared in the spectra of the cluster conformers. Moreover, principal component analysis (PCA) assists to understand the feature of the simulated data and confirms the formation of the THDES. Solvent selectivity triangle (SST) of solvatochromic parameters also demonstrate that this THDES has some important properties similar to ionic liquids and common deep eutectic solvent.

## INTRODUCTION Drug delivery faces substantial challenges as many newly developed drug molecules have low solubility, bioavailability, and stability.¹ Developing a new drug molecule is enormously expensive. Therefore, various techniques such as amorphous solid dispersion, lyophilization, particle size reduction, complexation, salt formation, and solvent formation have emerged to improve solubility and bioavailability of the existing active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs).²,³ It is easily understandable that improving the bioavailability of already existing drugs is way more profitable than launching a new one.⁴

Ionic liquids (ILs) have received great attraction in recent years to develop a potential pathway applying its features to overcome some of the problems of drug delivery mentioned above.³ ILs have also been reported as drug delivery vehicles, such as formulation of microemulsions, improvement of dissolution, and enhancement of transdermal delivery of sparingly soluble drugs.⁵,⁶ However, due to the expensive production, high toxicity, and poor biodegradability, drug delivery by ILs has become a less attractive option over the time.⁷ A deep eutectic solvent (DES) is considered an
analogue of ILs and a potential alternative solvent with a wide range of applications with less drawbacks.⁸

In DES, a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) are mixed together, where significant depression of freezing point is one of the most common phenomena.⁹ Among different kinds of DESs, a therapeutic deep eutectic solvent (THDES) is a new type in which at least one of its components must be an API. Researchers successfully developed some THDESs to enhance their solubility, membrane transport, drug delivery, and bioavail- ability.¹⁰,¹¹ Formation of THDESs based on choline chloride, and menthol, combined with three different APIs including acetylsalicylic acid, benzoic acid, and phenylacetic acid were reported by Aroso and co-workers.¹¹ A few works have been reported on the basis of experimental studies and MD

Perkins and co-workers worked on choline chloride–urea eutectic solvent combining simulation and experiment.12 Comparing MD simulations and infrared spectrum, they suggested that a strong interaction between the NH2 of urea and the chloride anion occurs. They also studied three more choline chloride based eutectic solvents using the same methods and observed hydrogen bonding among the anions and HBDs, which agreed with their previous claim.13 Sun et al. studied 1:2 ChCl/urea (reline) using classical MD simulation and concluded that the spontaneous intercalation of urea molecules in the choline chloride crystal lattice disrupted the ordered structure.14 The simulated structure of the DES is in agreement with reported neutron diffraction structure.15 Liquid reline and its mixture with water have also been probed by Fetisov et al.16 and Shah et al.17 by employing different force fields. Although several experimental studies are available on the THDES, little to no work has been reported on their structural, thermodynamic, and intermolec- ular interactions of the THDES with computational and experimental insights.

In this work, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation and density functional theory (DFT) calculations are employed to unravel the atomic level interactions of choline chloride (ChCl) based THDESs. Combined MD and DFT studies can assist to explain arrangements, orientations, interactions, and vibrations in the THDES. 18-21 The aims of this study are to find answers of the following questions: (i) what are the orientations of ChCl and acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) while they form the THDES, (ii) how is the melting point significantly decreased after forming the THDES, and (iii) what are the driving forces? Both computational and experimental Raman and FT-IR spectroscopic techniques 19 are employed to observe the molecular vibrations and the formation of hydrogen bonds in the THDES. Principle component analysis (PCA) is used to explain the spectra of different cluster conformers of the studied THDES further. 22 Solvatochromism analysis, which explains transition energy (E_T^N) and Kamlet-Taft parameters (hydrogen bond donor acidity (α), hydrogen bond acceptor basicity (β), and polarizability (π*)^23) is incorporated as a complementary method to explain how the studied THDES is different from or similar to other DESs, ILs, and common organic solvents.

METHODS Computational Details. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation using the YASARA Dynamics²⁴ program was used to generate all possible cluster conformers of the THDES. Here, the Amber 14²⁵ force field was considered and the particle mesh Ewald (PME) method²⁶ was used for calculating the long-range electrostatic interactions. Five, ten, and twenty pairs of ChCl and ASA were simulated in the gas phase for 10 ns. For initial comparison, the atom—atom radial distribution for one nonboning interaction was calculated for all three systems. In all cases, the peak was found at the same distance with different probabilities, which is obvious as the number of pairs are different (Figure S1). Among them, five pairs could not demonstrate the broad scenario of the solvent system and 20 pairs seemed too complex. Moreover, for big clusters, other parameters are difficult to calculate. In 10 pairs, simulation represented all types of interactions clearly (Figure S2); therefore, ten pairs were selected as the representative sample of the DES system for further simulation. The system was simulated for 40 ns to generate the atom—atom radial

distribution function (RDF) of the system. The periodic boundary condition (cell box of 36.75 Å × 36.75 Å × 36.75 Å) and temperature of 298 K were considered using the NVT ensemble for all simulations. The system was minimized and equilibrated with the default protocol of YASARA dynamics. The time step of 1.25 fs was used and simulation snapshots were captured at every 100 ps. All simulations were repeated five times to reproduce the MD simulation results (Figure S3).

All quantum calculations were performed with the Gaussian 09 software package.²⁷ Gas phase equilibrium geometries of ChCl, ASA, and their most stable cluster conformers (generated from MD simulation) were fully optimized using the density functional theory (DFT) method, where the ωB97XD functional and 6-311++G(d,p) basis set were used to calculate the association energies of the clusters.²⁸ Changes of electronic energies, enthalpies, and the Gibbs free energies were also investigated to demonstrate the formation of strong nonbonding interactions between ChCl and ASA. Population analysis was carried out using the NBO method,²⁹ and the electrostatic potential derived charges were calculated employ- ing the CHELPG scheme.³⁰

Experimental Details. Materials. Nile red, 4-nitroaniline, N,N-diethyl-4-nitroaniline, and dichloromethane (DCM) were purchased from Thermo-Fischer Scientific (Dubuque, IA) as the UV–vis absorbance probes. Acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) and anhydrous choline chloride (ChCl) were purchased from Acros Organics, where all of the chemicals have purity ≥99% and analytical grade.

Synthesis of 1:1 ChCI/ASA THDES. ChCl/ASA (1:1) was formulated by mixing anhydrous choline chloride and acetylsalicylic acid in a 1:1 molar ratio at 80 °C for 3 h in a covered beaker under constant stirring 600 rpm at atmospheric pressure until a homogeneous liquid was obtained. After preparation, it was preserved in the desiccator because the compounds are highly hygroscopic.

FT-IR and Raman Spectroscopic Methods. A spectrum two PerkinElmer FT-IR spectrometer coupled with a LiTaO₃ (lithium tantalate) MIR detector was used to scan the 1:1 ChCl/ASA THDES sample. Spectra were recorded in transmission mode for an average of 20 individual scans in the spectral region 400–4000 cm⁻¹ with a resolution of 1 cm⁻¹ at room temperature. Background collection was done before every sampling, and data analysis was carried out using Origin Pro software version 9.0. The experiment was performed to analyze the presence of nonbonding intermolecular interactions between ChCl and ASA. For the analysis of solid ChCl and ASA, a Thermal Nicolet FT-IR 6700 was used with the same spectral region and resolution.

To measure the sensitivity of Raman spectrum of ChCl, ASA, and 1:1 ChCl/ASA, the HORIBA JobinYvon Raman (model-LabRAM 800HR) System was used, where spectral analysis was carried out by Origin Pro 9.0 software. The laser source (Green laser-MPC 6000) was powered on and the software linked to it was run in the computer. Samples were loaded at the sample holder and a 10x magnifying lens was focused on the samples, where the 530 nm wavelength laser (Green) was hitting over. The diffraction grating (300) and filter type were set via software to get the better scattered light for detection. In the case of the filter (D2), the lower the index was, the higher the intensity of scattered light would have been.

Solvatochromic Method. Individual solutions of 5 × 10⁻⁴ M Nile red, 4-nitroaniline, and N,N-diethyl-4-nitroaniline dyes were prepared in dichloromethane (DCM). An appropriate amount of the dye stock solutions was micropipetted into clean, dry glass vials to mix with 1:1 ChCl/ASA. The glass vials were then capped, vortexed, and mixed properly. ## ■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION **Radial Distribution Function (RDF) Analysis by MD Simulation.** To elicit the formation of eutectic solvents and their nonbonding interactions, the atom—atom radial distribution functions (RDFs) are calculated from MD simulations. RDF can be used to investigate the distances between two atoms in MD simulations, which gives the probability of

finding a particle at a certain distance from the reference particle compared to the statistical distribution.15 The atom–atom RDFs, which provided the atomic level insights into the overarching structure of the THDES system, are represented in Figure 1. The complex nature of ChCl and ASA with multiple H bonding or nonbonding sites produces broad peaks and poorly defined minima. Figure 1a illustrates the contact distances between the atoms of ChCl and ASA. The first peak is between chloride and the hydrogen (21) atom on −OH of ASA, which shows the contact distances between the hydroxyl hydrogen atom and chlorine anion. This tall and narrow peak demonstrates the presence of hydrogen bonding and the interaction is around 2.1 Å, which is consistent with the HBD interactions with chloride anion in other previously studied DES systems.12,13,33 It is known that the hydrogen bond strength can be correlated to the distance between hydrogen bond donor (HBD) and hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA).34 Figure 1a also shows the RDF of the chloride and the HBD atom (O13) of the ASA as well as the RDF of Cl− and OCh+ atom of choline cation. According to the RDFs, the distances between Cl−···OCh+ and Cl−···OASA are almost same, which signifies that Cl− is working as a bridge between ASA and Ch+. These phenomena are also confirmed from the simulation snapshots, depicted in Figure 2.

These simulations suggest that the disruption to cation– anion electrostatic attractions of ChCl by ASA and formation of highly interconnected hydrogen bonding in 1:1 ChCl/ASA could be one of the major rationales behind melting point depression. This disruption was estimated through the calculation of the N$^{+}$-Cl$^{-}$ radial distribution function, shown in Figure 1a. Two peaks are observed in this RDF, a strong peak at 4.2 Å and a weak interaction at 4.8 Å. Table S1 provides a list of hydrogen bond distances present in the cluster conformers and those are also labeled in Figure 4. The THDES system exhibits a highly interconnected hydrogen bonding network, wherein the ASA molecule interacts strongly with the Cl⁻ as well as the choline cation. Besides, the hydroxyl group of the carboxylic functionality on ASA interacts through the H···Cl⁻ H bond in all four conformers ranging from 1.98 to 2.10 Å. Analyzing F and Q conformers, it is found that the C= O end of the esteric functionality on ASA interacts with methyl protons on choline via C—H···π interactions with H···O distances of 2.35 and 2.29 Å, respectively. Moreover, in all four conformers, Cl⁻ is clearly acting as charge transfer bridge between the choline cation and ASA, which is further confirmed via charge transfer analysis.

**Charge Transfer Analysis.** According to a recent review on DESs, charge delocalization between the anion and HBDs is occurring via hydrogen bonding interactions, which is actually responsible for the depression of freezing point of DESs. 36 Again, the strength of natural and ionic hydrogen bond corelates with the amount of charge transfer (NBO) from the HBA to the HBD.37

The CHELPG partial charge analysis and NBO charge analysis were employed to investigate this proposed charge delocalization in our THDES system. Four different representative conformers were analyzed. As can be seen in Table 1, the charge of chloride is significantly reduced (ranging from -0.723 to -0.780) in all investigated conformers along with the net increase in the negative charge on the ASAs ranging from -0.042 to -0.075 according to CHELPG partial charge analysis. The same pattern of the results is observed in the case of NBO charge analysis as well. Comparing the charge distribution in the THDES system with its components reveals that the positive charge at the cationic core is increasing and the negative charge at the hydroxyl group of choline is decreasing. These analyses give clear evidence that both of the functional groups are essential for the charge transfer occurring among the choline cation, chloride anion, and acetylsalicylic acid molecule through hydrogen bonding and electrostatic interactions.

Experimental and Calculated Raman and FTIR Spectra Analysis. Acetylsalicylic acid is an an acetyl derivative of salicylic acid. Therefore, this compound should have two peaks between 1650 and 1850 cm⁻¹ on its IR spectra for its acid and ester group.³⁸ In the 1:1 ChCl/ASA spectrum, two peaks in that range have been observed, where 1673 cm⁻¹ corresponds to carboxylic acid group and 1751 cm⁻¹ represents the ester group. However, both of the peaks are broadened and merged together due to the nonbonding intermolecular interactions between the ChCl and ASA. However, the peak for the —OH group of ChCl¹² was also broadened between 3135 and 3690 cm⁻¹ in the spectrum of 1:1 ChCl/ASA, indicating strong H bonds between the —OH of ChCl and ASA (Figure 5b). Besides, in the range 900–980 cm⁻¹, the quaternary ammonium group³⁹ should show a characteristic peak. ## CONCLUSION In this study, we have investigated the interactions between ChCl and ASA in the THDES by combined computational and experimental techniques. Analyzing RDF data generated from MD simulations demonstrates that there are several hydrogen bonds between ChCl and ASA, especially between the -OH of ASA and Cl⁻ of ChCl. Density functional theory calculations show that Cl⁻ is acting as a charge transfer bridge between Ch⁺ and ASA, which is observed in RDF analysis. The CHELPG partial charge analysis and NBO charge analysis reveal that the positive charge at the cationic core and the hydroxyl group of Ch⁺ have been decreased and transferred to ASA through the chloride bridge. Kamlet—Taft parameters, α, β, and π*, experimentally confirmed that Cl⁻ plays the most important role to transfer charges in the hydrogen bonding network of the THDES. Thermochemical data acquired from the DFT calculation proved the spontaneity of the formation of its conformers.
Experimental Raman and IR spectra of 1:1 ChCl/ASA are compared with the spectra of ChCl and ASA. Some of the

peaks of the ChCl and ASA spectra are nearly disappeared or are merged in the spectrum of 1:1 ChCl/ASA, which is the clear indication of hydrogen bond formation or the formation of the THDES. The computed Raman and IR spectra showed similar features; however, computed spectra show more peaks compared to the experimental spectra. Hence, it is difficult to differentiate the peaks located below 2000 cm⁻¹ or specifically the peaks of the fingerprint region. Principal component analysis not only effectively assists to compare the spectra of ChCl, ASA, and the four cluster conformers of 1:1 ChCl/ASA of that region but also demonstrates that the spectral features of ChCl and ASA are totally distinctive and the conformer's spectral features are between those of ChCl and ASA. The results obtained from this study can be summarized in three points: (i) MD simulation generates the representative conformers, which show the possible orientations of the microstructures of ChCl/ASA. (ii) Radial distribution function (RDF) and spectral data analyses confirm that the hydrogen bonding and the interaction patterns involved in the system cause the depression of the melting point. (iii) DFT calculations and solvatochromic parameters provide the information about charge dislocation, which is the major driving force for the formation of the THDES. In summary, this work shows in-depth atomic level understanding of how a THDES is formed.

Therefore, various techniques such as amorphous solid dispersion, lyophilization, particle size reduction, complexation, salt formation, and solvent formation have emerged to improve solubility and bioavailability of the existing active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs).²,³ It is easily understandable that improving the bioavailability of already existing drugs is way more profitable than launching a new one.⁴ Ionic liquids (ILs) have received great attraction in recent years to develop a potential pathway applying its features to overcome some of the problems of drug delivery mentioned above.³ ILs have also been reported as drug delivery vehicles, such as formulation of microemulsions, improvement of dissolution, and enhancement of transdermal delivery of sparingly soluble drugs.⁵,⁶ However, due to the expensive production, high toxicity, and poor biodegradability, drug delivery by ILs has become a less attractive option over the time.⁷ A deep eutectic solvent (DES) is considered an analogue of ILs and a potential alternative solvent with a wide range of applications with less drawbacks.⁸ In DES, a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) are mixed together, where significant depression of freezing point is one of the most common phenomena.⁹ Among different kinds of DESs, a therapeutic deep eutectic solvent (THDES) is a new type in which at least one of its components must be an API. Perkins and co-workers worked on choline chloride–urea eutectic solvent combining simulation and experiment.12 Comparing MD simulations and infrared spectrum, they suggested that a strong interaction between the NH2 of urea and the chloride anion occurs. Although several experimental studies are available on the THDES, little to no work has been reported on their structural, thermodynamic, and intermolec- ular interactions of the THDES with computational and experimental insights. In this work, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation and density functional theory (DFT) calculations are employed to unravel the atomic level interactions of choline chloride (ChCl) based THDESs. Combined MD and DFT studies can assist to explain arrangements, orientations, interactions, and vibrations in the THDES. 18-21 The aims of this study are to find answers of the following questions: (i) what are the orientations of ChCl and acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) while they form the THDES, (ii) how is the melting point significantly decreased after forming the THDES, and (iii) what are the driving forces? Both computational and experimental Raman and FT-IR spectroscopic techniques 19 are employed to observe the molecular vibrations and the formation of hydrogen bonds in the THDES. Principle component analysis (PCA) is used to explain the spectra of different cluster conformers of the studied THDES further. 22 Solvatochromism analysis, which explains transition energy (E_T^N) and Kamlet-Taft parameters (hydrogen bond donor acidity (α), hydrogen bond acceptor basicity (β), and polarizability (π*)^23) is incorporated as a complementary method to explain how the studied THDES is different from or similar to other DESs, ILs, and common organic solvents. METHODS Computational Details. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation using the YASARA Dynamics²⁴ program was used to generate all possible cluster conformers of the THDES. Here, the Amber 14²⁵ force field was considered and the particle mesh Ewald (PME) method²⁶ was used for calculating the long-range electrostatic interactions. Five, ten, and twenty pairs of ChCl and ASA were simulated in the gas phase for 10 ns. For initial comparison, the atom—atom radial distribution for one nonboning interaction was calculated for all three systems. In all cases, the peak was found at the same distance with different probabilities, which is obvious as the number of pairs are different (Figure S1). Among them, five pairs could not demonstrate the broad scenario of the solvent system and 20 pairs seemed too complex. Moreover, for big clusters, other parameters are difficult to calculate. In 10 pairs, simulation represented all types of interactions clearly (Figure S2); therefore, ten pairs were selected as the representative sample of the DES system for further simulation. The system was simulated for 40 ns to generate the atom—atom radial distribution function (RDF) of the system. The periodic boundary condition (cell box of 36.75 Å × 36.75 Å × 36.75 Å) and temperature of 298 K were considered using the NVT ensemble for all simulations. The system was minimized and equilibrated with the default protocol of YASARA dynamics. The time step of 1.25 fs was used and simulation snapshots were captured at every 100 ps. All simulations were repeated five times to reproduce the MD simulation results (Figure S3). All quantum calculations were performed with the Gaussian 09 software package.²⁷ Gas phase equilibrium geometries of ChCl, ASA, and their most stable cluster conformers (generated from MD simulation) were fully optimized using the density functional theory (DFT) method, where the ωB97XD functional and 6-311++G(d,p) basis set were used to calculate the association energies of the clusters.²⁸ Changes of electronic energies, enthalpies, and the Gibbs free energies were also investigated to demonstrate the formation of strong nonbonding interactions between ChCl and ASA. Population analysis was carried out using the NBO method,²⁹ and the electrostatic potential derived charges were calculated employ- ing the CHELPG scheme.³⁰ Experimental Details. Materials. Nile red, 4-nitroaniline, N,N-diethyl-4-nitroaniline, and dichloromethane (DCM) were purchased from Thermo-Fischer Scientific (Dubuque, IA) as the UV–vis absorbance probes. Acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) and anhydrous choline chloride (ChCl) were purchased from Acros Organics, where all of the chemicals have purity ≥99% and analytical grade. Synthesis of 1:1 ChCI/ASA THDES. ChCl/ASA (1:1) was formulated by mixing anhydrous choline chloride and acetylsalicylic acid in a 1:1 molar ratio at 80 °C for 3 h in a covered beaker under constant stirring 600 rpm at atmospheric pressure until a homogeneous liquid was obtained. Analyzing RDF data generated from MD simulations demonstrates that there are several hydrogen bonds between ChCl and ASA, especially between the -OH of ASA and Cl⁻ of ChCl. Density functional theory calculations show that Cl⁻ is acting as a charge transfer bridge between Ch⁺ and ASA, which is observed in RDF analysis. The CHELPG partial charge analysis and NBO charge analysis reveal that the positive charge at the cationic core and the hydroxyl group of Ch⁺ have been decreased and transferred to ASA through the chloride bridge. Kamlet—Taft parameters, α, β, and π*, experimentally confirmed that Cl⁻ plays the most important role to transfer charges in the hydrogen bonding network of the THDES. Thermochemical data acquired from the DFT calculation proved the spontaneity of the formation of its conformers. Experimental Raman and IR spectra of 1:1 ChCl/ASA are compared with the spectra of ChCl and ASA. Some of the peaks of the ChCl and ASA spectra are nearly disappeared or are merged in the spectrum of 1:1 ChCl/ASA, which is the clear indication of hydrogen bond formation or the formation of the THDES. The computed Raman and IR spectra showed similar features; however, computed spectra show more peaks compared to the experimental spectra. Hence, it is difficult to differentiate the peaks located below 2000 cm⁻¹ or specifically the peaks of the fingerprint region. Principal component analysis not only effectively assists to compare the spectra of ChCl, ASA, and the four cluster conformers of 1:1 ChCl/ASA of that region but also demonstrates that the spectral features of ChCl and ASA are totally distinctive and the conformer's spectral features are between those of ChCl and ASA. The results obtained from this study can be summarized in three points: (i) MD simulation generates the representative conformers, which show the possible orientations of the microstructures of ChCl/ASA. (ii) Radial distribution function (RDF) and spectral data analyses confirm that the hydrogen bonding and the interaction patterns involved in the system cause the depression of the melting point. (iii) DFT calculations and solvatochromic parameters provide the information about charge dislocation, which is the major driving force for the formation of the THDES. In summary, this work shows in-depth atomic level understanding of how a THDES is formed. ## ASSOCIATED CONTENT **Ⓢ Supporting Information** The Supporting Information is available free of charge at https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jpca.0c00851. Analyzing RDF data generated from MD simulations demonstrates that there are several hydrogen bonds between ChCl and ASA, especially between the -OH of ASA and Cl⁻ of ChCl. Density functional theory calculations show that Cl⁻ is acting as a charge transfer bridge between Ch⁺ and ASA, which is observed in RDF analysis. The CHELPG partial charge analysis and NBO charge analysis reveal that the positive charge at the cationic core and the hydroxyl group of Ch⁺ have been decreased and transferred to ASA through the chloride bridge. Kamlet—Taft parameters, α, β, and π*, experimentally confirmed that Cl⁻ plays the most important role to transfer charges in the hydrogen bonding network of the THDES. Thermochemical data acquired from the DFT calculation proved the spontaneity of the formation of its conformers. Experimental Raman and IR spectra of 1:1 ChCl/ASA are compared with the spectra of ChCl and ASA. Some of the peaks of the ChCl and ASA spectra are nearly disappeared or are merged in the spectrum of 1:1 ChCl/ASA, which is the clear indication of hydrogen bond formation or the formation of the THDES. The computed Raman and IR spectra showed similar features; however, computed spectra show more peaks compared to the experimental spectra. Hence, it is difficult to differentiate the peaks located below 2000 cm⁻¹ or specifically the peaks of the fingerprint region. Principal component analysis not only effectively assists to compare the spectra of ChCl, ASA, and the four cluster conformers of 1:1 ChCl/ASA of that region but also demonstrates that the spectral features of ChCl and ASA are totally distinctive and the conformer's spectral features are between those of ChCl and ASA. The results obtained from this study can be summarized in three points: (i) MD simulation generates the representative conformers, which show the possible orientations of the microstructures of ChCl/ASA. (ii) Radial distribution function (RDF) and spectral data analyses confirm that the hydrogen bonding and the interaction patterns involved in the system cause the depression of the melting point. (iii) DFT calculations and solvatochromic parameters provide the information about charge dislocation, which is the major driving force for the formation of the THDES. In summary, this work shows in-depth atomic level understanding of how a THDES is formed. ## ASSOCIATED CONTENT **Ⓢ Supporting Information** The Supporting Information is available free of charge at https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jpca.0c00851.
